danish.title: Fjortende bog (1812) — Kapitel 9
paragraphs: Efter at have taget franske kapper og chakotter på red Petja og Dolokhov til den lysning, hvorfra Denisov havde rekognosceret den franske lejr, og da de kom ud af skoven i bælgmørke, red de ned i lavningen. Da de nåede bunden, sagde Dolokhov til de kosakker, der ledsagede ham, at de skulle vente dér, og red videre i hurtig trav langs vejen mod broen. Petja, med hjertet oppe i halsen af spænding, red ved hans side.
»Hvis vi bliver taget, lader jeg mig ikke fange levende! Jeg har en pistol,« hviskede han.
»Lad være med at tale russisk,« sagde Dolokhov i et hastigt hvisken, og i netop det øjeblik hørte de gennem mørket udfordringen: »Qui vive?« * og klikket fra en musket.
* »Hvem der?«
Blodet steg Petja til kinderne, og han greb sin pistol.
»Lanciers du 6-me,« * svarede Dolokhov uden at sætte hestens tempo op eller ned.
* »Lanserer fra 6. regiment.«
En vagtposts sorte skikkelse stod på broen.
»Mot d'ordre.« *
* »Feltråb.«
Dolokhov trak i tøjlerne og red frem i skridt.
»Dites donc, le colonel Gérard est ici?« * spurgte han.
* »Sig mig, er oberst Gérard her?«
»Mot d'ordre,« gentog vagtposten, idet han spærrede vejen og ikke svarede.
»Quand un officier fait sa ronde, les sentinelles ne demandent pas le mot d'ordre...« råbte Dolokhov pludselig ophidset og red lige mod vagtposten. »Je vous demande si le colonel est ici.« *
* »Når en officer gør sin runde, beder skildvagterne ikke om feltråb... Jeg spørger, om obersten er her.«
Og uden at vente på svar fra vagtposten, der var trådt til side, red Dolokhov op ad stigningen i skridt.

Da han bemærkede den sorte silhuet af en mand, der krydsede vejen, standsede Dolokhov ham og spurgte, hvor kommandanten og officererne var. Manden, en soldat med en sæk over skulderen, standsede, kom helt hen til Dolokhovs hest, rørte ved den med hånden og forklarede ligefremt og venligt, at kommandanten og officererne var længere oppe ad bakken til højre i gården ved bondegården, som han kaldte godsejerhuset.

Da de var redet op ad vejen, på begge sider af hvilken der kunne høres fransk snak rundt om lejrbålene, drejede Dolokhov ind i godsejergården. Da han var redet ind, steg han af og gik hen mod et stort, flammende lejrbål, hvor flere mænd sad og talte højlydt. Noget kogte i en lille kedel ved kanten af bålet, og en soldat i en spids hue og blå kappe, belyst af ilden, knælede ved siden af den og rørte rundt i indholdet med en ladestok.
»Åh, han er en hård nød at knække,« sagde en af officererne, der sad i skyggen på den anden side af bålet.
»Han skal nok få gang i dem, de fyre!« sagde en anden med et grin.
Begge blev tavse og stirrede ud i mørket, da de hørte lyden af Dolokhovs og Petjas skridt, idet de nærmede sig bålet med deres heste.
»Bonjour, messieurs!« * sagde Dolokhov højt og tydeligt.
* »Goddag, mine herrer.«
Der blev uro blandt officererne i skyggen bag bålet, og en høj officer med lang hals gik rundt om bålet og hen til Dolokhov.

»Er det dig, Clément?« spurgte han. »Hvor fanden...?« Men da han opdagede sin fejltagelse, afbrød han sig selv og hilste med en rynket pande på Dolokhov som en fremmed, idet han spurgte, hvad han kunne gøre for ham.

Dolokhov sagde, at han og hans ledsager forsøgte at indhente deres regiment, og henvendte sig til hele selskabet med spørgsmålet, om de vidste noget om 6. regiment. Ingen af dem vidste noget, og Petja syntes, at officererne begyndte at se på ham og Dolokhov med fjendtlighed og mistænksomhed. I nogle sekunder var alle tavse.
»Hvis I regnede med aftensuppen, er I kommet for sent,« sagde en stemme bag bålet med et undertrykt grin.
Dolokhov svarede, at de ikke var sultne og måtte videre den nat.

Han overgav hestene til den soldat, der rørte i gryden, og satte sig på hug ved bålet ved siden af officeren med den lange hals. Officeren tog ikke øjnene fra Dolokhov og spurgte igen, hvilket regiment han tilhørte. Dolokhov, som om han ikke havde hørt spørgsmålet, svarede ikke, men tændte en kort fransk pibe, som han tog op af lommen, og begyndte at spørge officeren om, hvor langt vejen foran dem var sikker for kosakker.
»De banditter er overalt,« svarede en officer bag bålet.
Dolokhov bemærkede, at kosakkerne kun var en fare for efternølere som hans ledsager og ham selv, »men de ville vel næppe vove at angribe større afdelinger?« tilføjede han spørgende. Ingen svarede.
»Nå, nu går han snart,« tænkte Petja hvert øjeblik, mens han stod ved lejrbålet og lyttede til samtalen.

Men Dolokhov genoptog den samtale, der var gået i stå, og begyndte at stille direkte spørgsmål om, hvor mange mand der var i bataljonen, hvor mange bataljoner, og hvor mange fanger. Da han spurgte om de russiske fanger i det detachement, sagde Dolokhov:

»Hvilket hæsligt besvær at slæbe de her lig rundt med sig! Det ville være bedre at skyde det rak,« og han brød ud i højlydt latter, så mærkelig at Petja troede, franskmændene straks ville gennemskue deres forklædning, og han trådte uvilkårligt et skridt tilbage fra lejrbålet.

Ingen svarede et ord på Dolokhovs latter, og en fransk officer, som de ikke kunne se — han lå indsvøbt i en kappe — rejste sig og hviskede noget til en kammerat. Dolokhov rejste sig og kaldte på den soldat, der holdt deres heste.
»Bringer de mon vores heste eller ej?« tænkte Petja, mens han instinktivt rykkede tættere på Dolokhov.
Hestene blev bragt.
»God aften, mine herrer,« sagde Dolokhov.

Petja ville gerne sige »god nat«, men kunne ikke få et ord frem. Officererne hviskede indbyrdes. Dolokhov var længe om at komme op på sin hest, der ikke ville stå stille, og så red han ud af gården i skridt. Petja red ved hans side og længtes efter at kigge sig over skulderen for at se, om franskmændene løb efter dem, men vovede det ikke.

Da de kom ud på vejen, red Dolokhov ikke tilbage over det åbne land, men gennem landsbyen. Ét sted standsede han og lyttede. »Hører du?« spurgte han. Petja genkendte lyden af russiske stemmer og så de mørke skikkelser af russiske fanger rundt om deres lejrbål. Da de var kommet ned til broen, red Petja og Dolokhov forbi vagtposten, som uden et ord gik mut frem og tilbage, og derefter red de ned i lavningen, hvor kosakkerne ventede på dem.
»Nå, farvel. Sig til Denisov: 'ved det første skud ved daggry,'« sagde Dolokhov og gjorde mine til at ride væk, men Petja greb fat i ham.
»Virkelig!« råbte han. »Du er sådan en helt! Åh, hvor det er flot, hvor det er pragtfuldt! Hvor jeg elsker dig!«

»Det er godt, det er godt!« sagde Dolokhov. Men Petja slap ham ikke, og Dolokhov kunne i mørket se, at Petja bøjede sig mod ham og ville kysse ham. Dolokhov kyssede ham, lo, vendte sin hest og forsvandt i mørket.

english.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Having put on French greatcoats and shakos, Petya and Dolokhov rode to the clearing from which Denisov had surveyed the French camp. Emerging from the forest into pitch darkness, they descended into the hollow. At the bottom, Dolokhov told the Cossacks accompanying him to wait there and rode on at a quick trot toward the bridge. Petya, his heart pounding with excitement, rode beside him.
'If we're caught, I won't be taken alive! I have a pistol,' he whispered.
'Don't speak Russian,' said Dolokhov in a hurried whisper, and at that very moment came the challenge from the darkness: 'Who goes there?' and the click of a musket.
('Who goes there?')
The blood rushed to Petya's face and he gripped his pistol.
'Lancers of the Sixth!' Dolokhov replied, neither quickening nor slowing his horse's pace.
('Lancers of the Sixth Regiment.')
The black shape of a sentinel stood on the bridge.
'Password.'
('Password.')
Dolokhov reined in his horse and walked it forward.
'Tell me, is Colonel Gerard here?' he asked.
('Tell me, is Colonel Gerard here?')
'Password,' the sentinel repeated, blocking the way without answering.
'When an officer is making his rounds, sentinels don't ask for the password!' Dolokhov suddenly barked, riding straight at the sentinel. 'I'm asking you if the colonel is here!'
('When an officer is making his rounds, sentinels don't ask for the password. I'm asking you if the colonel is here.')
And without waiting for an answer from the sentinel, who had stepped aside, Dolokhov rode up the slope at a walk.

Noticing the dark outline of a man crossing the road, Dolokhov stopped him and asked where the commander and officers were. The man—a soldier with a sack over his shoulder—stopped, came close to Dolokhov's horse, touched it with his hand, and explained simply and in a friendly way that the commander and officers were up the hill to the right, in the courtyard of the farm (as he called the landowner's house).

Having ridden up the road with French conversation audible around campfires on both sides, Dolokhov turned into the courtyard of the landowner's house. He dismounted and approached a large, blazing campfire around which several men sat talking noisily. Something was boiling in a small cauldron at the fire's edge, and a soldier in a peaked cap and blue overcoat, lit up by the flames, was kneeling beside it stirring the contents with a ramrod.
'Oh, he's a tough one,' said one of the officers sitting in the shadow on the other side of the fire.
'He'll make those fellows get a move on!' said another, laughing.
Both fell silent, peering into the darkness at the sound of Dolokhov's and Petya's footsteps approaching with their horses.
'Good evening, gentlemen!' Dolokhov said loudly and clearly.
('Good evening, gentlemen.')
There was a stir among the officers in the shadows, and one tall, long-necked officer walked around the fire toward Dolokhov.
'Is that you, Clement?' he asked. 'Where the devil—?' But catching his mistake, he broke off and, with a frown, greeted Dolokhov as a stranger, asking what he could do for him.

Dolokhov said that he and his companion were trying to catch up with their regiment and, addressing the group, asked whether anyone knew anything about the Sixth Regiment. No one knew anything. Petya thought the officers were beginning to eye him and Dolokhov with hostility and suspicion. For several seconds, no one spoke.
'If you were hoping for the evening soup, you've come too late,' said a voice from behind the fire, with a suppressed laugh.
Dolokhov replied that they weren't hungry and had to keep moving through the night.

He handed the horses to the soldier stirring the pot and squatted on his heels by the fire next to the long-necked officer, who kept staring at him and again asked what regiment he belonged to. Dolokhov, as if he hadn't heard, didn't answer. Instead, lighting a short French pipe he'd taken from his pocket, he began asking the officer how safe the road ahead was from Cossack attacks.
'Those bandits are everywhere,' replied an officer from behind the fire.

Dolokhov observed that Cossacks were only dangerous to lone stragglers like himself and his companion, 'but surely they wouldn't dare attack large detachments?' he added, as if seeking confirmation. No one responded.
'Well, now he'll leave,' Petya thought every moment as he stood by the fire listening.

But Dolokhov picked up the dropped conversation and began asking direct questions: how many men in the battalion, how many battalions, how many prisoners? Asking about the Russian prisoners in their column, Dolokhov said:

'Terrible nuisance dragging those corpses around! Better to shoot that rabble,' and he burst into such loud, strange laughter that Petya was sure the French would see through their disguise at any second. He involuntarily stepped back from the fire.

No one responded to Dolokhov's laughter. A French officer they couldn't see—lying wrapped in a greatcoat—sat up and whispered something to a companion. Dolokhov stood, called for the soldier holding their horses.
'Will they bring the horses, or won't they?' thought Petya, instinctively moving closer to Dolokhov.
The horses were brought.
'Good evening, gentlemen,' said Dolokhov.

Petya wanted to say 'Good night' but couldn't get the words out. The officers were whispering together. Dolokhov took a long time mounting his horse, which wouldn't stand still, then he rode out of the yard at a walk. Petya rode beside him, longing to look back to see if the French were following but not daring to.

Coming out onto the road, Dolokhov didn't ride back across the open ground but through the village. At one spot he stopped and listened. 'Do you hear?' he asked. Petya recognized the sound of Russian voices and saw the dark shapes of Russian prisoners huddled around their campfires. When they descended to the bridge, Petya and Dolokhov rode past the sentinel, who paced silently and morosely up and down, then dropped into the hollow where the Cossacks were waiting.
'Well then, goodbye. Tell Denisov: at the first shot, at daybreak,' said Dolokhov and was about to ride off, but Petya grabbed his arm.
'Really!' he cried. 'You're such a hero! Oh, how wonderful, how splendid! How I love you!'

'All right, all right!' said Dolokhov. But Petya wouldn't let go, and through the gloom Dolokhov saw him leaning forward, wanting to kiss him. Dolokhov kissed him, laughed, wheeled his horse around, and vanished into the darkness.
